clue.text: Awkward sod, Tim Henman, getting a reprimand

indicators.note: something awkward is clumsy and out of order, so the letters that follow are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: The former British tennis star gets told off by some awkward character.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Henman was Britain's leading tennis player around 2000; his name, with sod, supplies every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns describe a stern telling-off given to someone for poor behaviour.

clue.text: Some want iPod, especially in the UK and New Zealand?

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the answer is a run of letters inside the next words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning these three words

explanation.surface: Plenty of people in Britain and New Zealand would like an Apple music player.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain and New Zealand lie on almost opposite sides of the globe, so each is the other's antipodes; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodes are places diametrically opposite each other on the earth, which Britain and New Zealand roughly are.

clue.text: An incorrect character in London-to-Leeds road race

parts.note: the M1 motorway runs from London to Leeds, with the 1 read as the letter I
a short fast race

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about a race along a motorway contains a typo.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway; its digit 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a wrong letter or symbol printed by mistake, a typographical error.

clue.text: Homes for Robin and Jay, perhaps?

definitions.text: Homes for Robin and Jay, perhaps?

parts.words: Homes for Robin and Jay, perhaps?
parts.note: surface reading: houses where two people called Robin and Jay live
setter's reading: the robin and the jay are both birds, so their homes are what birds build

explanation.surface: Estate agent's listing of properties for a couple named Robin and Jay.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds such as robins and jays live and raise their young in twig-built structures.

clue.text: Synopsis of plot beginning to shift Conservative policy

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter alone, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of shift
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
a party line is its official policy

explanation.surface: A summary of a political scheme to move Conservative policy in a new direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyline is the sequence of events in a narrative, i.e. a summary of its plot.

clue.text: Manufacturers of extreme bits of magenta kitchenware — ridiculous!

indicators.note: the extreme bits of a word are its two ends, so each word keeps only its first and last letters

parts.note: first and last letters of magenta
first and last letters of kitchenware
first and last letters of ridiculous

explanation.surface: A sneer at firms that make garish purple pots and pans.
explanation.walkthrough: All three of the last words are trimmed to their ends, not just the first two.
explanation.definitionFit: Makers are those who produce goods, the same as companies that manufacture things.

clue.text: Indian regularly ignored assent from German warrior

indicators.note: ignoring letters at a regular interval drops every other one, leaving alternate letters

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of Indian
ja is the German word for yes

explanation.surface: An Indian fighter's agreement was overlooked by a German soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninja was a Japanese fighter trained in covert warfare and martial arts.

clue.text: Attack American president no. 41 or 43

parts.note: Am. is a standard abbreviation for American
George H. W. Bush was the 41st US president and his son George W. the 43rd

explanation.surface: A call to attack one of the two Bush presidents.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'or' is fair because both numbered presidents share the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise attack from a hidden position, used here as a verb meaning to attack.

clue.text: Drug dealers losing head, or theatre workers

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: slang for people who sell illegal drugs

explanation.surface: Either beheaded drug dealers or theatre staff, a grim choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ushers are staff who show audience members to their seats in a theatre or cinema.

clue.text: Oddly, mean to host activity for summer?

indicators.note: oddly means taking the odd-numbered positions, the first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: Someone stingy plans to throw a summer-holiday party.
explanation.walkthrough: Summer reads as the season, but here it is one who sums, adding numbers up.
explanation.definitionFit: A summer, pronounced like 'drummer', is a person doing sums, and that work is arithmetic in the British school subject.

clue.text: High cost with monarch's hosiery

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and muddled, so the next word's letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
a king is a monarch, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: Royal hosiery comes at a steep price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High cost' reads as one phrase about price; High is the anagram signal for cost alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockings are close-fitting leg coverings, a type of hosiery.

clue.text: Court judges politician with fury in America

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so the first pieces go within the country

parts.note: the United States
Member of Parliament
ire is anger

explanation.surface: An angry American politician lays into the judiciary.
explanation.walkthrough: Court suggests a law court, but these are officials at a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: Umpires officiate matches such as tennis, ruling on play from the side of the court.

clue.text: Distance, say, a horse-drawn cart goes to the west

indicators.note: in an across answer west is leftward, so travelling west reads the letters right to left

parts.note: e.g., for example
taken as written
a dray is a low cart pulled by horses, traditionally for beer barrels

explanation.surface: A horse and cart heads west over some distance.
explanation.definitionFit: Yardage is a distance or length measured in yards, as in American football.

clue.text: Like a pleasure-seeker in the disco, dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places, giving a new order

parts.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A party-lover dancing the night away in a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist lives for pleasure, so the adjective describes that self-indulgent outlook.

clue.text: Trained tiger cats, using a cunning plan

indicators.note: trained animals are drilled into new positions, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Circus big cats taught to follow a clever scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Strategic describes acting according to a carefully devised plan to gain an advantage.

clue.text: Girl left behind, as Americans say

parts.note: standard abbreviation for left
the American slang word for the buttocks

explanation.surface: A young woman abandoned, in the American phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: Behind looks like part of 'left behind', but it means the backside, for which Americans say ass where Britons say arse.
explanation.definitionFit: Lass is a mainly Scottish and northern English word for a young woman.

clue.text: Bizarrely cool Paris citadel many tourists visit

indicators.note: bizarrely means in a strange, irregular way, so the letters come out in an odd order

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A traveller's verdict that a much-visited Parisian fortress is oddly cool.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris suggests a French landmark; the citadel is in Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acropolis is the ancient hilltop citadel of Athens, among Greece's most visited sights.

clue.text: In shop, Tim is this person with a half-full glass?

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer sits inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning these four words

explanation.surface: A shopworker called Tim who always looks on the bright side.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on the saying that a cheerful person sees the glass as half full rather than half empty.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hopeful and positive is said to see a glass as half full, the classic image of looking on the bright side.

clue.text: Disorder in dining room

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an untidy state, chaos
second meaning: where members of the armed forces eat together

explanation.surface: Chaos breaks out at the dinner table.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an untidy jumble and a military canteen where officers or soldiers take meals.

clue.text: Planet, hardly empty, with soggy ground

parts.note: the red planet

indicators.note: an empty word has its insides removed, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: first and last letters of hardly

explanation.surface: A planet that is barely bare yet has boggy terrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Marshy land is wet and waterlogged, describing terrain made up of bog or swamp.

clue.text: Complimentary strong drink for a non-conformist

parts.note: complimentary means given without charge
a spirit is a distilled alcoholic drink such as whisky

explanation.surface: A free shot of liquor handed to a rebel.
explanation.definitionFit: A free spirit lives independently and ignores convention, much like a nonconformist.

clue.text: Batter is extremely tough and impetuous

indicators.note: extremely is read as at the extremes, so only the end letters of the next word count

parts.note: first and last letters of tough
rash means acting without thought

explanation.surface: A cricketer at the crease is described as very hard and hot-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: Batter looks like a noun for a cricketer or baseball player; it is the verb meaning to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrash someone is to beat them hard and repeatedly, the same as battering them.

clue.text: Attack flipping idiot, in trouble

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the turned word goes within the other

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: An angry outburst against a fool who is in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: Flipping reads like a British mild curse ('flipping idiot'), but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is to attack violently, physically or with words.

clue.text: Return to clergyman, crossword setter and model

parts.note: short for Reverend
the setter refers to themself as I
to sit for a portrait is to model

explanation.surface: A vicar, the puzzle compiler and a fashion model all head home.
explanation.definitionFit: To revisit a place or topic is to go back to it again.

clue.text: Party very upset — Kamala drained alcoholic drink

indicators.note: in a down answer, upset means turned upside down, so the letters run bottom to top

parts.note: a do is a party
standard abbreviation for very

indicators.note: a drained word has had its contents emptied, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: first and last letters of Kamala

explanation.surface: At a very fraught party, Kamala Harris downs a stiff drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Vodka is a clear distilled spirit, originally from Russia and Poland.

clue.text: Captain Scott's starter — smoked fish

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of Scott
a kipper is a smoked herring

explanation.surface: Captain Scott's first course on his expedition is smoked herring.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Scott led the doomed Antarctic expedition; here Captain is the definition and starter means first letter, not a first course.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the captain of a ship or the leader of a sports team.

clue.text: Son with French bread where tapas may be served

parts.note: standard abbreviation for son
pain is French for bread

explanation.surface: A boy eating French bread in a tapas bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapas are small savoury dishes, a tradition of the country on the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Flowery shrub from Hyde Park employee, as some say

indicators.note: what some people say is spoken, so the answer matches the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: a ranger looks after a park, here London's Hyde Park

explanation.surface: A flowering bush supplied by a London park worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is a large royal park in central London; 'as some say' admits the sound match is loose, with the final R dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: The hydrangea is a garden shrub bearing large rounded heads of pink, blue or white flowers.

clue.text: What lazy person does, spreading lies about Democrat

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so these letters go around the other piece
spreading things scatters them about, so the letters of the word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for a Democrat

explanation.surface: A layabout spends their time spreading falsehoods about a Democrat politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lazy idles, passing time doing nothing useful.

clue.text: Trips in Tulsa Chilean organised

indicators.note: organising things puts them into a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A Chilean in Oklahoma arranges some journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: Trips looks like journeys, but it is the slang verb for experiencing a drug high.
explanation.definitionFit: To trip is slang for having drug-induced visions, which is to see things that are not there.
